writing.explanation:
A problem is a good match for Permutation Backtracking when it asks for orderings and assignment sequences. Here the concrete task is: Return the number of permutations of four distinct items. The visible input `[1,2,3,4]` is an example, not a definition of the whole problem. Ask what operations the solution must support and what the input guarantees. Use it when constraints prune combinations early and the task asks for one or all valid constructions. The right choice follows from those guarantees, not from a familiar noun in the prompt.

The decisive invariant is: Choose one unused item for the next position, recurse, then mark it unused again. Try to say why it applies to the task without quoting the implementation. Which fact becomes known after one update, and which possible answers remain? Most patterns here explore a decision tree; meet-in-the-middle instead enumerates two halves and combines them. Define the partial choice or subset summary that the pattern retains. If that claim cannot be maintained on a legal input, the pattern is wrong or one of its preconditions is missing. A counterexample is more useful than a vague warning: change one property of the sample, trace the first two steps, and identify the exact claim that fails.

Compare costs before committing. The advertised bound is O(n*n!) time · O(n) state excluding output; identify the operation responsible for it and the extra memory it needs. Then compare a straightforward alternative: a direct scan, full sort, or repeated recomputation may be easier but can pay for the same work many times. Do not choose the more elaborate method just because it has a famous name. For the sample, predict `24` and explain which part of the state lets the method reach that result.

When the prompt is ambiguous, ask about input size, ordering, duplicates, and required output format. Test no solution, one solution, duplicate inputs, and the order in which candidates are tried if output order is observable. For recursive search, push a choice, recurse, then undo it; for meet-in-the-middle, collect each half before matching them. In Rust, clone a path only when storing a completed answer. The Rust sketch can show a useful primitive without proving that the whole task is solved; connect each primitive to the requested output. You should be able to name a fitting case, a near miss, and the assumption separating them before writing the first line.
